claims.claim: The narrative of cultural criticism concerning the relation of natural and artificial converts into a narrative of political philosophy when contextualized through Arendt's earlier work, The Origins of Totalitarianism.
qualifications: Requires contextualization within Arendt's oeuvre and her previous book, The Origins of Totalitarianism
claims.supporting_excerpt: Following the argumentation of The Human Condition concerning the relation of nat - ural and artificial we arrived to a turning point where the narrative of cultural criti - cism converts into the narrative of political philosophy.

claims.claim: Totalitarianism represents the end-result of processes of re-naturalization that aimed to annihilate human personality, spontaneity, and free action in order to change the human race into an animal species.
qualifications: Required an arsenal of new technologies including modern telecommunication, psycho-technologies, and organizational-institutional technologies
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is important concerning the subject of this paper that totalitarianism was the end-result of the processes of re-naturalization. For the introduction of this unprec - edented political form an arsenal of new technologies was needed.

definitions.definition: An unprecedented political form that served as the end-result of processes of re-naturalization, utilizing telecommunication, psycho-technologies, and organizational-institutional technologies to annihilate human personality and individuality.

distinctions.distinction: The Human Condition focuses on the relation of natural and artificial from a cultural criticism perspective that implicitly carries forward the threat of re-naturalization, whereas The Origins of Totalitarianism directly addresses imperialism and the historical genesis of totalitarianism as a process.

must_not_be_lost: The transition from cultural criticism to political philosophy relies on connecting The Human Condition with The Origins of Totalitarianism.
Totalitarianism is interpreted as the extreme consequence of re-naturalization processes that threaten the man-made artificial world.
parsed.segment_function: To trace the transition from cultural criticism to political philosophy by examining how Hannah Arendt's treatment of the natural and artificial in The Origins of Totalitarianism informs her later arguments in The Human Condition regarding re-naturalization and totalitarian threats.
unresolved_context: The full scope of the reconstruction of the ramifying chain of ideas from The Origins of Totalitarianism is acknowledged as beyond the possibilities of the paper.
